title: Why losing hurts more than winning feels good
summary: Loss aversion is the tendency for losses to weigh more than equal gains. It shapes how we react to fees, discounts and investments — though its size is more debated than pop psychology suggests.
evidenceNote: Loss aversion is one of the most cited ideas in behavioral economics, but recent research debates how general it is: the effect appears weaker or absent for small, everyday stakes.

scenes.text: A coin flip: lose 100 kr on tails, win 150 kr on heads. Would you take it?
scenes.answer: Many people say no — even though, on average, the bet pays.

scenes.text: Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky called this loss aversion: losses tend to feel bigger than equal gains.
Classic estimates suggested losses weigh about twice as much as gains.

scenes.reveal: The effect varies a lot — and for small stakes it may be weak or absent.

left.label: Framing
left.text: A 'fee' often stings more than a missed 'discount'

right.label: Investing
right.text: People sell winners early and cling to losers

scenes.text: Ask: would I decide the same if it were framed as a gain?
